For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.

arxiv:2611.19563.title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
arxiv:2611.19563.abstract: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.

arxiv:2611.19566.title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
arxiv:2611.19566.abstract: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. arxiv:2611.19572.title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
arxiv:2611.19572.abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

arxiv:2611.19575.title: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
arxiv:2611.19575.abstract: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. We instead propose a DFL framework that achieves risk-sensitive behavior while retaining point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time. Starting from the dual representation of the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and adding entropy regularization, we derive a smooth surrogate for the CVaR of regret. Its gradient induces an instance-dependent reweighting within each minibatch that emphasizes high-risk outcomes, so the approach can turn existing surrogate-loss DFL methods, including the SPO+ loss, into risk-sensitive variants. When instantiated with SPO+, the resulting objective admits a generalization bound on the CVaR of the true regret. Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems show substantial reductions in tail regret when the uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.

arxiv:2611.19586.title: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
arxiv:2611.19586.abstract: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.

arxiv:2611.19587.title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
arxiv:2611.19587.abstract: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order $k$ of the velocity renders the $D$-dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if $2k > D$ and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.

arxiv:2611.19588.title: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
arxiv:2611.19588.abstract: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

arxiv:2611.19597.title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
arxiv:2611.19597.abstract: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints. We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure. NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

arxiv:2611.19609.title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
arxiv:2611.19609.abstract: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. H2' (description-paraphrase consistency of name-free states not lower in failure items) is mixed: the SmolLM2 deficit test is significant under the pre-registered specification but not robust; Phi-3 non-inferiority holds across margins and a word-overlap covariate, although its bootstrap interval includes zero; Qwen2-0.5B is inconclusive. A capacity explanation remains untested. We report vehicle-level signals only, not meaning.

arxiv:2611.19624.title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
arxiv:2611.19624.abstract: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

arxiv:2611.19625.title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
arxiv:2611.19625.abstract: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

arxiv:2611.19634.title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
arxiv:2611.19634.abstract: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

arxiv:2611.19649.title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
arxiv:2611.19649.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

arxiv:2611.19650.title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
arxiv:2611.19650.abstract: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

arxiv:2611.19656.title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
arxiv:2611.19656.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

arxiv:2611.19658.title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
arxiv:2611.19658.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

arxiv:2611.19676.title: Score-Based Stochastic Closure Modeling via Offline Indirect Learning and Online Data Assimilation
arxiv:2611.19676.abstract: Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.

arxiv:2611.19681.title: RIFT: Reward Improvement Field Transfer for Cross-Domain Offline RL
arxiv:2611.19681.abstract: Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. We propose Reward Improvement Field Transfer (RIFT), which instead learns how low- and high-reward source transitions differ. RIFT encodes source and target transitions in a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions using optimal transport, and fits an affine field to their displacements. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. The approach builds on the hypothesis that related domains can share useful low-to-high reward structure despite different dynamics. We bound synthesis error under shared class geometry, identify conditions favoring target anchoring over source-high transplant, and derive a conditional connection to downstream return. Experiments on dense-reward locomotion tasks under gravity, morphology, and friction shifts show improved aggregate performance over existing baselines.

arxiv:2611.19686.title: Elicited Adaptation: Auditable Localized Fairness via Pairwise Queries
arxiv:2611.19686.abstract: How much must a predictor's scores change when a community's elicited fairness standard changes? Similarity and tolerance judgments define protected comparisons and acceptable score gaps. We study minimum uniform score movement on a fixed pool of $n$ profiles. For scores satisfying a source standard, we characterize the exact cost of retaining that standard during adaptation: runs of consecutive target constraints along shortest paths determine the optimal amplification factor. Its sharp worst case is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, and a full cost curve describes finite target-only repair budgets. Committing before the target is known can cost $n-1$ times the worst repair after revelation, even within one fixed convex ball of two-dimensional Mahalanobis metrics. Positive edge-budget floors cap both factors; bounded geometry also limits the commitment cost. At two interior targets of the construction attaining the $n-1$ bound, similarity queries alone yield a feasible $2$-approximate repair for tolerance $\eps\le1/[2(n-1)]$, reducing movement relative to common repair by a factor linear in $n$. Feasible $(1+\alpha)$-optimal repair on this family has worst-case tolerance-query complexity $\Theta(\alpha^{-2}n^2\log(1/\delta))$ under a fixed-slope logistic model. The analysis separates the information needed for a substantial adaptation benefit from the precision needed for nearly optimal movement. Elicitation studies and training comparisons examine tolerance choice and the relation between numerical compliance and predictive utility.

arxiv:2611.19692.title: MathaMAGICal: Validating Trajectory Data Attribution During Capability Acquisition
arxiv:2611.19692.abstract: Influence-function-based methods like MAGIC provide exact first-order scores for trajectory data attribution, yet only retraining indicates whether those scores accurately predict data removal. We evaluate MAGIC on $86$M- and $152$M-parameter GPT-2-style models learning multistep arithmetic from scratch on filtered web text and four synthetic math families. Full-run attribution at $86$M suffers from numerical overflow, and even with metagradient clipping, scores correlate near chance with retraining (linear datamodeling score, LDS, $0.17$--$0.22$). In contrast, short checkpoint windows yield stable, accurate predictions at both scales (LDS $0.86$--$0.99$ across four $100$-step windows at $152$M), whereas a single-checkpoint gradient-dot baseline shows near-zero correlation. Rankings of individual training blocks predict retraining only within that single run and do not transfer across seeds or hyperparameters ($\rho \le 0.09$), whereas format-level patterns replicate across runs. Two data families, worked examples and primitive facts, occupy $2.1$--$2.6\times$ their corpus share in both the helpful and harmful $5\%$ score tails, reflecting strong bidirectional local sensitivity distinct from net benefit under multi-epoch family deletion. These results show that trajectory attribution is reliable within short, validated windows and yields family-level insights that generalize across runs.

arxiv:2611.19698.title: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
arxiv:2611.19698.abstract: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.

arxiv:2611.19700.title: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
arxiv:2611.19700.abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

arxiv:2611.19701.title: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift
arxiv:2611.19701.abstract: Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning. We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity. More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels.

arxiv:2611.19733.title: Sample-Efficient Ensemble Reinforcement Learning at Scale
arxiv:2611.19733.abstract: Ensemble methods such as MeanQ have been shown to improve the sample efficiency of relatively small model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) architectures, including DQN and similarly sized variants such as Rainbow. However, to our knowledge, the effects of ensembling on large-scale architectures such as Bigger Better Faster (BBF) have not been studied. In this work, we present MeanQ-BBF, a hybrid model-free algorithm that combines the principles of MeanQ and BBF. Through statistically rigorous evaluation on the Atari 100K benchmark, we show that in contrast to naive scaling of the network size of BBF, which degrades performance, MeanQ-BBF is able to leverage the increase in model capacity to improve performance over BBF. Moreover, MeanQ-BBF does this in a computationally efficient way by organizing the added parameters into largely independent learners. Finally, we discuss the performance-cost tradeoff in the context of practical sample-efficient RL.

arxiv:2611.19742.title: Exploration of Reinforcement Learning in Generative Recommendation Models
arxiv:2611.19742.abstract: Traditional cascaded recommender systems balance accuracy and efficiency over large item spaces, but misaligned stage-wise objectives hinder end-to-end optimization. Generative recommendation unifies these stages in an autoregressive framework, providing a natural interface for reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the entire generation process. However, directly applying RL often leads to unstable optimization and degraded recommendation quality. We revisit Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and other ratio-based objectives through a unified logit-gradient view. We identify three issues: (i) clipped surrogates create dead-gradient regions, under-utilizing samples; (ii) negative-advantage updates can become effectively unbounded as importance ratios grow, allowing a small subset of negatives to dominate optimization; and (iii) ratio-based control lacks sensitivity to absolute policy confidence, so updates on high-confidence cases may fail to vanish. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose \emph{Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization} (GBPO), a simple objective with stop-gradient normalization that is simultaneously (a) fully gradient-active, (b) sign-symmetrically bounded for both positive and negative updates, and (c) explicitly confidence-weighted under current policy probabilities. This ensures that updates gracefully vanish for $\pi\!\to\!1$ positives and $\pi\!\to\!0$ negatives. Across the evaluated settings, GBPO achieves competitive recommendation performance with more stable training than competing RL methods.

arxiv:2611.19762.title: When Does an AUROC Comparison Survive a Change in Population Mix?
arxiv:2611.19762.abstract: Does an AUROC comparison survive a change in the proportions of tasks, populations, or image corruptions? A pooled-AUROC ranking of failure detectors or uncertainty scores describes one particular mix of groups. We study two fixed scores for a common binary target under mixtures of fixed group-conditional laws. Using the cross-group AUC decomposition, we prove that every rational symmetric quadratic comparison geometry is realizable by finite scalar-score distributions. Universal dominance is thus coNP-hard, and even exhaustive checks of every mixture on fewer than $K$ groups can miss a $K$-group reversal. A grid bound gives a dimension-uniform approximation certificate with sharp $1/m$ order. Common score marginals across groups make the comparison numerator linear, with an error envelope for imperfect alignment. These results yield exact finite-bank audits, explicit reversal mixtures and distances, and simultaneous population statements. For failure detection with a frozen ResNet-50 on ImageNet-C, 15 of 18 confidence-score comparisons win in every corruption family on a discovery split, and all 15 are finite-bank certified over all family mixtures on a held-out split; over all 15 corruption types, of 14 discovery winners the corrected grid certifies 10, leaves 3 unresolved, and finds one confirmation reversal of at least 0.05 AUROC. An audit of all 11,019 released Stable LM 2 12B outputs and 35 uncertainty methods finds 66 confirmation-set comparisons that win within all four tasks yet reverse under mixing. Discovery-fitted marginal rank alignment removes all 66; an alignment-error envelope certifies 83 comparisons. Label checks also change several selected reversals. The findings distinguish robustness of frozen scores from robustness after calibration; they do not establish human-error detection, robustness to unseen corruptions, or generalization beyond the evaluated banks.

arxiv:2611.19768.title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
arxiv:2611.19768.abstract: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG.

arxiv:2611.19770.title: Exact Sparse Assignment with Costly Target Embeddings: Fixed-Realization Certificates and an Empirical Audit
arxiv:2611.19770.abstract: Embedding-based one-to-one association is common in vision and data integration: detections are associated with tracks and records are linked across databases. Such pipelines often solve a sparse optional assignment whose edge scores add a cheap term to an inner product of neural embeddings. When target embeddings are costly, one can acquire them selectively and stop once a certificate proves that the current assignment is optimal. We give such a certificate for unit-norm embeddings. It bounds the unknown part of every reassignment by a support function and maximizes the resulting robust gains with a second sparse assignment; a shared owner-centred bound dominates any fixed-centre triangle bound. We make precise what is certified when network features are not batch-invariant: the realized values of the acquired rows and every unit-ball completion of the rest, not a second forward pass in a different batch. Auditing against a separately batched cache tests a different property; on our first pilot it produced a spurious $2.49\times10^{-6}$ objective failure. We audit the corrected protocol on four public text entity-matching benchmarks with two frozen encoders; no image data is used. All 96 certificate simulations and 120 online selective timings were exact on their own realization (largest objective gap $6.82\times10^{-13}$). At group size 8 the shared certificate acquires on average 60% of candidate-active targets, against 74% (mean centre), 69% (MEB) and 60% (zero centre): it beats the mean and MEB centres but not the zero centre, and savings concentrate in one benchmark (7% acquired). The prespecified runtime claim is contradicted: selective execution is +0.510 s slower per run (dataset-cluster 95% interval [+0.248, +0.772]). Uniform-microbatch re-encodings preserved the optimum in only 5 of 8 encoder-dataset cells, and 45 of 120 online runs disagreed with an eager cache at near-ties.

arxiv:2611.19784.title: How Should Parallel Langevin Chains Share Noise?
arxiv:2611.19784.abstract: Parallel Langevin sampling usually draws an array of independent Gaussian vectors, one row per chain. The average row drives the ensemble mean, with variance $1/K$ per coordinate for $K$ chains. Yet the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) specifies only each row's distribution. Subtracting the column means and rescaling, as in classical antithetic sampling, makes that variance zero. Each chain keeps its ordinary ULA path law for any finite run. For quadratic targets we derive the joint covariance of linear estimates computed from the ensemble mean, including coefficient estimates, time averages and predictions. The identity separates contributions from initial states and Gaussian draws. The coupling changes the second through one scalar, which is zero whenever the draws sum to zero across chains. For nonquadratic targets we bound the remaining variance. Centering has a price: for a quadratic form in the mean-subtracted Gaussian state, the ensemble average has variance $1/(K-1)$ relative to one chain, compared with $1/K$ under independent draws. On three tempered logistic posteriors, eight centered chains reduced the variance of the posterior-mean estimate, summed over coordinates, by two to three orders of magnitude compared with eight independent chains. They also beat 128 independent chains on variance and on variance times sampling time. Under Metropolis correction the reduction shrank to about three- to eightfold: rejected draws no longer balance accepted ones. The measured variance ratios were consistent with a leading-order prediction from rejection frequency and noise energy.

arxiv:2611.19794.title: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
arxiv:2611.19794.abstract: Research taste is increasingly discussed in the context of AI scientists, yet remains little studied or measured in LLMs. This judgment matters especially in open-ended research, where a direction must be chosen before a verifiable objective is available. We operationalize research taste through one task of the scientific workflow: choosing which future research direction to pursue given a research goal and current results. Rather than predicting downstream scientometric metrics or treating author choices as objectively correct, we evaluate models against human-authored future-work directions and report author alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral measures of research-direction preference. We construct an order-controlled evaluation of 80 pairwise comparisons from 19 ML papers published between December 2025 and February 2026 across four subdomains. Each query presents a research goal, hypotheses tested with key results, and two candidate future directions: one author-recommended direction and one plausible distractor sampled from a similar paper. Across eight LLMs, author alignment ranges from 45.0% to 67.5%, while stable divergence ranges from 15.0% to 36.2%. These divergences largely persist under similarity controls, prompt ablations, and an author-preference framing check, and inter-model agreement suggests that some non-author preferences are shared across models. We characterize what models diverge toward using transition-category labels and selected reasoning examples, finding recurring movement toward scaling/generalization and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure/data extensions. We view this as an early descriptive evaluation for eliciting research taste profiles in LLMs, and as a step toward understanding and steering their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in novel open-ended scientific discovery.

arxiv:2611.19796.title: The Sense Paradigm for World Models
arxiv:2611.19796.abstract: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.

arxiv:2611.19798.title: Barron Approximation and locally optimal weight densities for shallow neural networks
arxiv:2611.19798.abstract: Mean field theories provide optimization results for shallow neural networks by analyzing the weight distribution in infinite width limits. Corresponding results for finite sized networks are obtained by particle approximations, for which sharp quantitative bounds are still an open problem. In this paper, we consider a modified mean field loss, which allows a more fine grained control over finite sized networks. We prove convexity and equidistribution properties, which directly lead to Barron type approximation results for networks sampled from local loss minimizers. We demonstrate that particle approximations of the new loss function naturally lead to gradient descent methods with dropout type regularization.

arxiv:2611.19800.title: Multi-Branch Transformer
arxiv:2611.19800.abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.

arxiv:2611.19812.title: Reasoning in the loop: antibody lead optimization by probing mechanism and measurement
arxiv:2611.19812.abstract: Lab-in-the-loop systems, in which a model proposes molecules, automated assays measure their properties and the results retrain the model, are a popular approach to antibody lead optimization. These systems optimize for a specification defined with metrics computed from instrument signals, so their success depends on how well those metrics serve as proxies for the properties a drug candidate needs. When a metric is a poor proxy, neither a better model nor more data will fix it, and identifying the problem usually requires expert review. We report two campaigns run on BigHat Biosciences' Milliner platform, one on an anti-albumin nanobody (VHH) and one on an anti-mesothelin single-chain variable fragment (scFv), in which a research team and a general-purpose AI agent, Claude, brought scientific reasoning into the loop. Over seven rounds and about 1,010 design variants we built libraries from antibody lineage, structure and biophysics, and found from the raw curves that on each scaffold one thermal metric did not measure what its name implied. The libraries were built as controlled comparisons, so the results also show what each mutation contributes to each property. We fit a physical model of the curves, used it to choose metrics suited to each scaffold, and changed the experimental protocol, varying protein concentration and heating rate, to test the model against pre-registered predictions. Both leads improve on their parents in affinity, thermal stability and aggregation while improving or maintaining yield and purity.

arxiv:2611.19815.title: Conditional Optimal Transport and Triangular Maps for Imitation Learning
arxiv:2611.19815.abstract: We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.

arxiv:2611.19821.title: GraphPass: A Study of Graph Neural Networks for Compiler Pass Selection
arxiv:2611.19821.abstract: Compiler pass selection is usually governed by fixed pipelines (-O2, -O3) or hand-written heuristics. We study whether a graph neural network (GNN) over a program's control-flow graph (CFG) can select among a fixed menu of five pass sequences in a single forward pass. GraphPass encodes each CFG with a graph attention (GAT) or graph convolutional (GCN) encoder and classifies it into one of the five sequences. On a synthetic benchmark of 5,000 generated CFGs in five program families, both encoders agree with the benchmark's reference label on about 92% of held-out programs, versus 68.4% for a hand-written rule-based heuristic and 85% for a flat MLP. An edge ablation indicates that this gain comes from per-block processing rather than from CFG edges: a GCN given the same basic-block features with all edges removed scores 95.0%, versus 92.2% with the true CFG. In this benchmark the label is determined by the program family, so the task amounts to family recognition. Real-compiler speedup is not measured. Inference costs O(|V| + |E|) per CFG, measured at 1.7 ms for a typical program and about 0.8 s for a 100,000-block graph on one CPU core.

arxiv:2611.19825.title: Foundation Pareto Flow Policy for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
arxiv:2611.19825.abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.

arxiv:2611.19826.title: Where Is Rank-1 DiM Refusal Intervenable in Multimodal LM Derivatives?
arxiv:2611.19826.abstract: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.

arxiv:2611.19848.title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
arxiv:2611.19848.abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.

arxiv:2611.19896.title: LoopSkim: Lossless Multi-Depth Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models
arxiv:2611.19896.abstract: Looped language models such as Ouro and Raven apply one weight-shared block several times per token, so autoregressive decoding (AR) runs every loop of every token in sequence. Pipelined self-speculative decoders overlap these loops by drafting tokens from shallow readouts and verifying them at full depth. Yet every loop of a looped LM ends in a readout of the next token, and draft tokens pass through every depth anyway, so each depth can check them without an extra pass. We introduce LoopSkim, in which the depth of the pipeline is the verifier. Draft tokens copied from the context, as in prompt lookup decoding, enter after the first loops, any later readout that contradicts one replaces it at that depth, and only full-depth readouts commit tokens. LoopSkim fixes the random draws of every position in advance, so each check compares two tokens and decoding stays lossless in exact arithmetic under sampling for any number of checks and draft chains. Without training, its speedup over AR averages 1.73x that of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling, and its checks between the first loops and full depth speed it up on every model. An optional draft head adds a second chain and raises this average to 1.99x.

arxiv:2611.19911.title: "Don't Leave the Task Unfinished": Persistence-Driven Violations under Quiet Oversight
arxiv:2611.19911.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly given long, multi-step tasks to carry out, with the user reviewing little of what happens in between. Persistence, the tendency to keep working until a task is complete, is installed on purpose to improve performance on long tasks. Long-horizon tasks are typically complex, and the user's instruction can fall short of what the work actually requires, or conflict with the constraints the agent encounters in the task. We study what persistence does on long-horizon operations tasks that cannot be solved without breaking a documented constraint. We find that the agent pursues completion to the point of violating the constraint, and that a critically engaged user lowers the violation rate. Persistence takes violations from 29.2% to 58.3% across four models. Violations stay high wherever oversight goes quiet, whether the user is silent, assenting, or delegating with expressed trust. Only a questioning user, who asks for the basis of each action before allowing the next, brings the rate back to roughly the level measured without persistence. Practitioners should treat high persistence as a setting that carries a safety cost, and should recognize that the cost appears when oversight goes quiet. Safety here is better cast as a property of the human-AI pair than of the model alone. Project page: https://francis21c.github.io/quiet-oversight/

arxiv:2611.19917.title: Delayed Heuristic-Behavior-Target Coupling for Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning in Inventory Control
arxiv:2611.19917.abstract: Many reinforcement learning methods tie data collection to the task policy, while coordinating independently optimized behavior and target policies remains challenging. Policies learned by these methods can perform unreliably in long-horizon tasks under uncertainty, such as inventory control, where failures can incur extreme costs. We introduce Heuristic Behavior Policy Optimization (HBPO), an off-policy framework that routes heuristic guidance through persistent behavior learning, coupled with target-policy, updating separately with residual-based advantage estimation and emphatic weighting. Under matched environment interaction budgets on DSIS and its risk-augmented variant DSIS-RB, HBPO recovers many high-cost initial policies and improves most non-collapse comparison groups. Cold starts achieve competitive costs without final cost collapse across all tested seeds. We identify a transmission chain in the delayed heuristic-behavior-target coupling as a key driver of recovery and improvement. Generation-level diagnostics trace heuristic uptake and subsequent selective target responses, while component ablations support the contribution of this transmission mechanism to policy recovery and improvement.

arxiv:2611.19925.title: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD
arxiv:2611.19925.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.

arxiv:2611.19931.title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
arxiv:2611.19931.abstract: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.

arxiv:2611.19937.title: AllocFlow: End-to-End Portfolio Trading Action Generation from Raw Market Data
arxiv:2611.19937.abstract: Real-world portfolio management requires converting noisy market observations into coordinated, simultaneous allocations across multiple assets under shared capital constraints. Advances in forecasting models and alpha discovery help identify opportunities. However, traditional pipelines often decouple signal forecasting from portfolio construction, potentially misaligning learning with allocation and execution objectives. We present AllocFlow, an end-to-end flow-matching framework that directly generates joint portfolio allocations from raw multi-asset market histories. To capture dependencies among portfolio positions, AllocFlow employs a cross-asset flow Transformer conditioned on temporal market representations to generate continuous, signed position weights across all instruments jointly. To address the sample inefficiency and instability of learning continuous allocation policies from scratch, we establish a two-stage training scheme: strategy-supervised imitation shapes a structured distribution of candidate portfolios, followed by group-relative reinforcement learning (RL) that refines joint decisions using portfolio-level financial rewards and a frozen policy reference. On hourly cryptocurrency perpetual futures, RL refinement raises the annualized net return of the imitation policy from $27.79\%$ to $51.38\%$ and its Calmar ratio from $0.955$ to $4.043$, surpassing the teacher strategy on every metric, and AllocFlow reaches a Calmar ratio of $4.90$ on six further months of unseen 2026 data without retraining.

arxiv:2611.19965.title: Evaluating Near-Perfect Accuracy Claims in Machine-Learning-Based Leak Detection for Two-Phase Pipelines: A Condition-Blocked Audit
arxiv:2611.19965.abstract: Reliable leak detection in gas-liquid two-phase pipelines is important for process safety, yet machine-learning studies frequently report near-perfect performance using evaluation protocols that may not represent deployment to unseen operating conditions. This study audits a pressure-based leak-detection model using condition-blocked leave-one-condition-out validation, in which the classifier is tested on a flow condition excluded from training. Accuracy decreased from 93.3% under within-condition evaluation to 59.1% across fifteen unseen-condition tests. Ablation analysis showed that most of this difference arose from the data-splitting protocol, with a smaller contribution from encoding operating conditions as model inputs. Under condition-blocked evaluation, the false-alarm and missed-detection rates increased to 34.1% and 10.2%, respectively, demonstrating that near-perfect reported accuracy did not translate into reliable operation at unseen flow conditions. The reduction persisted across all evaluated classifiers, indicating that it was caused by the evaluation design rather than a particular model architecture. Grouped evaluation of an independent acoustic pipeline dataset produced a comparable reduction toward chance-level performance. These findings show that validation units must represent the conditions encountered during deployment. Condition-blocked evaluation and explicit reporting of operational error rates are therefore necessary before machine-learning leak detectors can support process-safety decisions.

arxiv:2611.19972.title: The structure of variational autoencoder latent spaces and its consequences for representation and optimization
arxiv:2611.19972.abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used to build low-dimensional representations of scientific data, with the expectation that regularization yields smooth coordinates for interpolation, generation and optimization. However, applications in microscopy reveal domains, narrow transitions and rare-state islands in VAE latent spaces that smoothness alone does not explain. We show that, for prototype data with squared-error reconstruction and an optimal decoder, the latent-space objective has a direct correspondence with the Flory-Huggins theory of a regular solution, and use it to analyze how the objective, posterior distributions and latent dimensionality organize the representation. Data families occupy domains separated by finite-width walls that broaden with increasing regularization until class separation is lost through posterior collapse. Class centroids behave like particles in a harmonic trap: the prior confines them, and structural dissimilarity sets a soft repulsion that determines which classes become neighbors and how far apart they sit, with separations growing only logarithmically with dissimilarity. Rare states can remain unresolved, form small islands, accumulate within walls or develop intervening domains, depending on their frequency and similarity to common states. The posterior covariance can align domains with the latent axes, but axis alignment does not imply separation of physical factors. Rotations can produce rings and encoder cuts that reflect data symmetry, while insufficient dimensionality can lead to suppression, mixing or folding of additional factors. Comparisons with flow models, deep kernel learning (DKL) and hybrid VAE-DKL models show how these structures change when reconstruction and prediction play different roles. We discuss implications for interpreting data, discovering rare states, generating intermediate states and optimizing properties.

arxiv:2611.19975.title: Federated Dataset Simulation: Inducing Label-Free Heterogeneity Across Tasks
arxiv:2611.19975.abstract: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across decentralized clients without sharing raw data. While the field has seen rapid growth, the datasets underpinning FL evaluation have not kept pace: real federated datasets remain scarce, and most studies rely on small-scale centralized classification datasets partitioned via Dirichlet label skew, a one-dimensional proxy for the multi-dimensional heterogeneity present in real federations. Moreover, label-based partitioning is by construction inapplicable to non-classification tasks such as segmentation and detection, for which no principled simulation method exists. We cast the conversion of centralized datasets into federated benchmarks as the task of Federated Dataset Simulation (FDS), and decompose it into a representation function $\Phi$ and an assignment mechanism $\pi$. We provide two label-free instantiations -- geometric partitioning via pretrained model embeddings and semantic partitioning via vision-language model-derived criteria -- applicable to classification and dense prediction tasks alike. We evaluate across four datasets spanning classification, segmentation, and detection, and show that both methods induce heterogeneity that matches or exceeds that of label-skew partitioning, with measurable impact on downstream FL performance. We release fds, a modular open-source package for end-to-end federated dataset simulation, heterogeneity measurement, and FL training, at https://github.com/siomvas/fds.

arxiv:2611.19985.title: When Zero Is Competitive: A Descriptive Pilot of Transformer and Gate-Graph Surrogates on Random-Angle Quantum Circuits
arxiv:2611.19985.abstract: We examine supervised classical prediction of all one-qubit Z and two-qubit ZZ expectation values on noiseless, layered 4-10-qubit RX/RY/RZ-CNOT circuits. In a 63-cell stratified workload with disjoint circuit-template tests, we evaluate one transformer encoder and gate-dependency graph neural networks against literal-zero and training-derived constant predictors. On the Arm K training labels, 44.89% of scalar targets have absolute magnitude below 0.05. The held-out-template zero predictor has equal-instance mean absolute error 0.193399, and none of the evaluated transformer checkpoints or final graph-network endpoints achieves a lower score.
